cls: Selective estrogen receptor modulator / protein kinase C inhibitor
pharm: Active metabolite of tamoxifen (4-hydroxy-N-desmethyl-tamoxifen) that potently antagonizes estrogen receptor-alpha and inhibits protein kinase C; given directly it bypasses the CYP2D6-dependent activation of tamoxifen.
tags: Investigational (oncology) / approved for bipolar mania in India
quick: Bipolar mania (per Indian approval): commonly 8 mg orally once daily; oncology dosing is investigational
Oral; taken once daily, generally consistent with respect to food
Mood/manic symptoms (psychiatric use); thromboembolism, endometrial and hot-flash effects (antiestrogen class)
summary: Endoxifen (4-hydroxy-N-desmethyl-tamoxifen) is the principal active metabolite of tamoxifen and a potent selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that also directly inhibits protein kinase C (PKC). It is NOT FDA-approved. Given directly, it bypasses the need for CYP2D6-mediated activation of tamoxifen, providing more predictable antiestrogen exposure - this has been studied in endocrine-refractory, ER-positive breast cancer and other ER-positive tumors (investigational, e.g., Z-endoxifen). Separately, because bipolar disorder is associated with overactive PKC signaling and endoxifen is a direct PKC inhibitor, oral endoxifen (typically 8 mg once daily) has been developed and approved in India for the treatment of acute mania in bipolar I disorder, with studies reporting reductions in Young Mania Rating Scale scores. Because dosing and indications derive from non-FDA (regional/investigational) sources, expected class effects mirror tamoxifen (hot flashes, venous thromboembolism, endometrial effects, antiestrogenic actions); clinicians should follow the applicable regional product information.
indications: Acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar I disorder (per regional - e.g., Indian - approval of oral endoxifen)
Investigational: endocrine-refractory ER-positive metastatic breast cancer and other ER-positive solid tumors (Z-endoxifen, clinical trials)
Note: NOT FDA-approved; uses are based on regional approval and clinical trial data

dosage.c: Bipolar I disorder - acute mania (regional approval)
dosage.d: Commonly 8 mg once daily (4 mg once daily also studied); follow the applicable national product information
Investigational dosing in clinical trials (e.g., Z-endoxifen at protocol-defined doses); not a marketed oncology dose

admin: Administer orally once daily as directed by the applicable regional product information
For the psychiatric (bipolar mania) indication, use as part of comprehensive management with monitoring of manic and depressive symptoms
Counsel on antiestrogen class risks (thromboembolism, endometrial effects) given its tamoxifen-metabolite pharmacology
Ensure pregnancy is excluded and effective contraception is used in females of reproductive potential
Follow the dose and schedule in the applicable national/clinical-trial documentation
moa: Endoxifen is the active metabolite of tamoxifen. As a selective estrogen receptor modulator it binds estrogen receptor-alpha (ER-alpha) with high affinity, blocks estrogen-driven transcription, and promotes ER-alpha degradation, inhibiting estrogen-dependent tumor cell proliferation (the basis for its antitumor activity). Independently of the estrogen receptor, endoxifen is a direct inhibitor of protein kinase C (PKC). Because bipolar mania is associated with overactive PKC intracellular signaling, PKC inhibition is the proposed mechanism for its antimanic effect. Administering endoxifen directly bypasses the variable CYP2D6-dependent conversion of tamoxifen, yielding more consistent active-drug exposure.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to endoxifen or tamoxifen
History of venous thromboembolism or stroke where antiestrogen therapy is inappropriate (class caution/contraindication)
relative: Endometrial hyperplasia/pathology or undiagnosed vaginal bleeding
Concurrent strong CYP-modulating or QT-affecting drugs (caution)
monitor: Psychiatric: manic and depressive symptom scales and clinical status
Signs of venous thromboembolism (leg swelling, chest pain, dyspnea)
Gynecologic symptoms / abnormal uterine bleeding (antiestrogen effect)

preg: Endoxifen, as an antiestrogen and active tamoxifen metabolite, is contraindicated in pregnancy because of the potential for fetal harm. Exclude pregnancy before starting and advise effective non-hormonal contraception during treatment.
lact: Breastfeeding is contraindicated during treatment because of the potential for serious adverse effects in the breastfed infant from an antiestrogenic agent.
renal: There are limited data on use in renal impairment; use with caution and monitor, as for other tamoxifen-related agents.
hepatic: Endoxifen is eliminated via hepatic metabolism; use with caution in hepatic impairment, where exposure may be increased.

major: Anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin) - tamoxifen-class agents can potentiate anticoagulant effect and bleeding risk
Other agents that increase thromboembolic risk - additive risk
moderate: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers - may alter endoxifen exposure
Aromatase inhibitors / other endocrine therapy - overlapping antiestrogen effects
minor: SSRIs that inhibit CYP2D6 (relevant for tamoxifen activation) are less relevant since endoxifen is the active form already
interactions.food: May be taken consistently with respect to food per regional guidance.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; no specific interaction data, but avoid heavy use.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor INR if on warfarin; perform gynecologic evaluation for abnormal bleeding.

serious: Venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism) - antiestrogen class effect
Endometrial changes/hyperplasia or, rarely, endometrial cancer (class effect with prolonged use)
rare: Mood changes / emergence of depressive symptoms (in bipolar use, monitor)
emergency: Acute pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis

monitoring: Psychiatric use: serial assessment of manic/depressive symptoms (e.g., YMRS/MADRS) and overall clinical response
Gynecologic symptoms and abnormal uterine bleeding
counsel: Take this medicine exactly as prescribed, once daily; do not stop suddenly without talking to your doctor
Report leg swelling/pain, sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, or signs of stroke (weakness, slurred speech) immediately - this drug can increase blood-clot risk
Women should report any unusual vaginal bleeding; use reliable non-hormonal birth control and do not breastfeed during treatment
Hot flashes are common; tell your doctor if they are bothersome
Keep follow-up appointments so your mood symptoms and side effects can be monitored
pk: Antimanic/clinical effects develop over days to weeks of dosing
Orally absorbed; peak plasma concentration within a few hours of dosing
Long - on the order of several days (similar to the tamoxifen metabolite range)
Store at room temperature, protected from moisture and light, per the regional product label
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - endoxifen is the active metabolite of tamoxifen; it is investigational in ER-positive cancers (Z-endoxifen) and APPROVED in India for acute bipolar mania (typically 8 mg/day)
Dual mechanism: potent estrogen-receptor-alpha antagonist (antitumor) and direct protein kinase C inhibitor (proposed antimanic effect, since bipolar mania involves overactive PKC)
Giving endoxifen directly bypasses variable CYP2D6-dependent activation of tamoxifen, giving more consistent active-drug levels
Antiestrogen class risks apply: venous thromboembolism, endometrial effects, hot flashes; contraindicated in pregnancy/lactation
Dosing and indications follow regional approval / clinical-trial protocols rather than US labeling
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered on the same day. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the once-daily schedule; do not double the dose. For the bipolar indication, do not discontinue abruptly without medical advice.
overdose: Specific human overdose data are limited. Expected effects relate to exaggerated antiestrogenic/tamoxifen-like pharmacology and possible neurologic or cardiac effects. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with monitoring for thromboembolic and cardiac events and symptomatic care. Seek specialist/poison-center guidance.
